Series::hypot¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::hypot(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::hypot_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::hypot_(const Series& rhs) const

What It Does¶

hypot() computes sqrt(a^2 + b^2) elementwise — the Euclidean length of the right triangle with legs a (the receiver) and b (other).

The reason it is a primitive rather than a two-line expression is range. The obvious spelling, (a.square() + b.square()).sqrt(), forms a^2 as an intermediate. If a is around 1e200, then a^2 is 1e400, which overflows float64 to inf, and the final sqrt returns inf even though the true answer is a perfectly ordinary 1e200.

hypot() avoids that by factoring out the larger magnitude first:

hi = max(|a|, |b|)
lo = min(|a|, |b|)
result = hi * sqrt(1 + (lo / hi)^2)

Now the squared term is (lo/hi)^2, which is always in [0, 1], so the intermediate never overflows unless the true result itself is out of range. When both inputs are 0 the result is 0 with no division by zero.

Shapes broadcast the same way as add(). The result dtype is floating point; an integer input is promoted.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The second leg b. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The elementwise hypotenuse. hypot_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

hypot() is differentiable. With h the output:

d/da hypot(a, b) = a / h
d/db hypot(a, b) = b / h

which are just the components of the unit vector pointing from the origin to (a, b). At a = b = 0 the derivative is defined here as 0 rather than 0/0.

In-Place Form¶

hypot_() is the in-place sibling of hypot(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — hypot_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 3.0}, {2});
auto y = pluss::make_series({4.0, 4.0}, {2});

x.hypot_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 5]

Examples¶

Example 1. Classic Pythagorean triples.

auto a = pluss::make_series({3.0, 5.0, 8.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 12.0, 15.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.hypot(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5.0000, 13.0000, 17.0000]

Example 2. The range-safety that motivates the method. The naive (a*a + b*b).sqrt() would overflow here; hypot() does not.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({3e200}).hypot(pluss::make_series({4e200})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[5.0000e+200]

Example 3. Both legs zero gives zero, not NaN.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0}).hypot(pluss::make_series({0.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000]

Example 4. other broadcasts. A scalar second leg is applied to every element.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({3.0, 5.0}).hypot(pluss::make_series(4.0)));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5.0000, 6.4031]

Example 5. The gradient is the unit direction vector.

auto a = pluss::make_series({3.0, 4.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 3.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.hypot(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.6, 0.8]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.8, 0.6]

For legs (3, 4) the hypotenuse is 5, and (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8).

Example 6. An integer input is promoted to a floating-point result.

auto a = pluss::make_series({3, 4}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
auto b = pluss::make_series({4, 3}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.hypot(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5.0000, 5.0000]

Example 7. Non-broadcastable shapes fail.

try {
  pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).hypot(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0}));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

broadcast: incompatible shapes

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • hypot() is the range-safe form on purpose. If you write (a.square() + b.square()).sqrt() yourself, you lose that safety.

  • A genuinely infinite result (for example hypot(inf, 1)) is still inf; only the spurious overflow from the intermediate square is removed.

  • The result is always floating point, even for integer inputs.

  • NaN in either input propagates.

Summary¶

hypot(a, b) is sqrt(a^2 + b^2) computed so the intermediate cannot spuriously overflow:

  • broadcasts like add(); always returns floating point

  • hypot(0, 0) = 0

  • differentiable, gradient (a/h, b/h) — the unit direction vector

See Also¶

  • Series::sqrt: the outer operation of the naive spelling hypot() replaces.

  • Series::atan2: the angle to go with this magnitude; together they are the polar form of (b, a).

  • Series::add: the broadcasting rules hypot() follows.
